ut.title: UT Inspection & Ultrasonic Thickness Testing | Dallas, TX
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing for Dallas, TX: wall thickness surveys, UT weld inspection of structural steel, piping and vessels. Request a Dallas UT quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Dallas, Texas
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic testing in Dallas, Texas: thickness measurement on piping, tanks and pressure vessels, and shear-wave examination of welds in structural steel, process piping and fabricated equipment. Dallas has no refinery row, but it does have a dense mix of steel fabricators, rail yards, pipeline and compressor facilities, power infrastructure and high-rise construction, and each needs ultrasonic data. Technicians are mobilized to your site and work to your procedure and code. Request a UT quote for Dallas and we reply within one business day.

Why Dallas UT work looks different from the Gulf Coast

Dallas sits inland, at the center of a metropolitan area that is large enough to behave like a regional industrial economy. The pressure on ultrasonic inspection comes less from corroding refinery piping and more from construction, manufacturing and transport. Steel fabricators in and around the city produce building frames, bridge girders, tanks and vessels, and they need weld inspection before pieces ship. Interstate and intrastate pipelines pass through North Texas with compressor stations and metering facilities that carry high-pressure piping. Rail cars, rail yards and bridges add cyclic load and fatigue. Electric transmission and substation structures need weld checks on towers and supports.

The result is a job mix where ultrasonic testing is as likely to be used on a groove weld in a structural steel connection as on wall loss in a process line. The first question to ask is what code governs the work, because the same probe and the same instrument will be used with very different acceptance rules.

Structural steel, bridges and high-rise frames

Ultrasonic examination of groove welds is a standard requirement for many building and bridge connections. AWS D1.1, the structural welding code for steel, includes ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds in its inspection clause, and AWS D1.5 governs steel bridge fabrication. The Texas Department of Transportation Dallas District serves Collin, Dallas, Denton, Ellis, Kaufman, Navarro and Rockwall counties, and major crossings such as the Margaret McDermott Bridge on I-30 over the Trinity River illustrate the scale of steel work in the area.

On a structural job, the technician scans full-penetration welds in flange and web connections, column splices and moment connections with angle-beam probes, usually at 45, 60 or 70 degrees chosen to match the weld geometry and plate thickness. Indications are classified by amplitude, length and location against the acceptance table in the code. Thickness checks on plate and on built-up members also use ultrasound when lamination or material loss is suspected. Because many structural welds are inspected soon after welding, the work is timed to the fabrication schedule and the cooling of the weld.

Pressure piping, vessels and tanks in the Metroplex

North Texas has process plants, gas processing and compression, chemical blending, food and beverage manufacturing, hospital and university boiler plants, and district heating and cooling equipment. These operate pressure systems that fall under ASME B31.3 for process piping, B31.1 for power piping and ASME Section VIII for vessels. Ultrasonic thickness measurement at condition monitoring locations tracks wall loss on elbows, tees, dead legs and reducers, and the readings are compared to the previous survey so the owner's inspector can set intervals.

Technique follows ASTM E797 and the thickness provisions of ASME Section V Article 5 and Article 23. Dual-element probes are used on corroded or pitted surfaces, and the instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same material before readings begin. Under API 510, API 570 and API 653, the owner's authorized inspector is the one responsible for the inspection program. Atlantis reports the data and does not act as that inspector. For tanks in North Texas terminals and storage yards, shell thickness at courses and nozzle areas is checked on request.

Welding codes and what the Dallas UT report must show

Ultrasonic acceptance changes with the code. ASME B31.3 provides for ultrasonic examination of production welds with criteria in Table 341.3.2. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12 covers ultrasonic examination of welds in vessels. API 1104 includes ultrasonic provisions for pipeline girth welds, and AWS D1.1 has its own rules for structural groove welds. Where ultrasonic testing is proposed to replace radiography, the owner, engineer and authorized inspector approve the substitution before the job.

The report names the component, the procedure and revision, the instrument, probe and reference block, the couplant, the surface condition and the scan plan. It lists each recordable indication by position, length and amplitude relative to the reference level, followed by accept or reject. For thickness work it includes the grid, nominal thickness, current and previous readings and the lowest measured value. See the national ultrasonic testing page and the ultimate guide to ultrasonic testing for general method information.

Texas rules that touch ultrasonic work

Texas regulates boilers and pressure vessels through the Texas Boiler Law, Chapter 755 of the Health and Safety Code, administered by the Department of Licensing and Regulation. Repairs and alterations follow the National Board Inspection Code and involve an authorized inspector. The Railroad Commission of Texas oversees intrastate pipeline safety under 49 CFR Parts 192 and 195 and its own rules, and interstate pipelines fall under PHMSA. Chemical and process plants with highly hazardous materials work under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(j), which requires inspection to recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice.

Which of these applies depends on the asset, and a short call usually settles it. The Texas inspection page lays out the sequence we follow from request to report.

People and procedures behind a UT job

Technicians are qualified under the company written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up the instrument, performs the scan and interprets results, while an ASNT Level III writes or approves the procedure and reviews the report. The Level III function is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If your company has its own written practice, we follow it. If it needs writing or revision, see written practice development and Level III consulting.

Rail, utility and heavy-lift steel

Dallas is a rail hub, and the steel that carries trains takes a beating that most buildings never see. Bridges, trestles and car structures see repeated stress cycles, so welds and plate near connections are checked for fatigue cracking and lamination. Ultrasonic thickness readings on plate and webs tell an owner whether section loss from corrosion has reduced the capacity of a member. Utility owners with transmission towers, substation frames and heavy-lift equipment ask for similar checks on baseplates, anchor connections and welded joints. These jobs often involve awkward access, such as the underside of a girder or the far face of a tower leg, so the scan plan is written around where the probe can actually reach.

When a weld can only be scanned from one side, the technician says so in the report, because a one-sided scan has a lower probability of finding a flaw that tilts away from the beam. The owner can then decide whether to accept the limitation, add another method or arrange better access. This kind of plain statement of what was and was not examined is worth more to an engineer than a long list of clean readings.

Instrument setup and surface condition

Before any ultrasonic work, the instrument is set up on a calibration block that matches the material and thickness range of the job. For thickness, the technician checks readings at both ends of the expected range, confirms the velocity setting and zeroes the probe. For weld examination, a reference level is established from side-drilled holes at the depths the scan will cover, and the beam index and angle are verified on a reference block. These checks are repeated at set intervals during the job and whenever the probe or cable is changed, and the results go in the report.

The surface needs to be smooth and clean enough for the probe to couple. Mill scale, weld spatter, loose paint and rust are removed locally, and the scanning surface beside a weld must be wide enough for the probe to travel the full skip distance. Rough cast surfaces and heavy blast profiles can need extra couplant or grinding. When access is limited, the report records any area that could not be scanned, so the owner knows precisely where coverage stopped.

Planning ultrasonic work in Dallas

Weather in Dallas swings hard. Summer afternoons routinely run above 100 degrees, and steel in the sun is far hotter than the air, which affects couplant and probe wear and may require high-temperature probes and a temperature correction on hot surfaces. Winter freezes, and occasionally ice, can stop outdoor work and change couplant behavior, so cold-rated couplant or enclosures are used. Spring storms and hail can interrupt scheduling at open fabrication yards.

The city's traffic and site security also matter. Fabricators, plants and construction sites ask for safety orientation before work, and construction sites change daily, so access to the weld may change between booking and arrival. We travel to your site and mobilize technicians from outside the city, so please give us the contact for gate procedures, lift or scaffold arrangements and any hot-work or confined-space permits.

UT, MT or PT for Dallas welds

Ultrasonic testing shows what is inside a weld and how much wall remains. For surface cracks on carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection in Dallas is often quicker, and for stainless or aluminum liquid penetrant testing in Dallas is the surface method of choice. Many structural welds are checked with a combination of visual, magnetic particle and ultrasonic examination. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, and the radiographic testing page for Dallas explains the alternatives.

Building your own UT team

Some Dallas employers want their own ultrasonic technicians. UT Level 1 training, UT Level 2 training and the UT practice simulator support that path, and ultrasonic testing training describes the syllabus. Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer certifies each technician. The Dallas training page shows how courses are arranged.

faq.q: What does Dallas ultrasonic weld inspection cover on structural steel?
faq.a: It covers full-penetration groove welds in beams, columns, splices and plates, examined with angle-beam probes against the acceptance criteria of the contract code, usually AWS D1.1 for buildings or AWS D1.5 for bridges.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic thickness testing be done while a pipe is in service?
faq.a: Yes, in most cases. The probe is placed on the outside surface with couplant. Hot lines need high-temperature probes and couplant, and the reading is corrected for temperature, so tell us the operating conditions.

faq.q: Does ultrasonic testing work through paint or coatings?
faq.a: Thin, well-bonded coatings are often acceptable, and the technician checks the reading against bare metal. Loose, blistered or thick coatings are removed locally because they distort readings and prevent proper coupling.

faq.q: Who decides remaining life after a UT thickness survey?
faq.a: The owner's inspector and engineer make that decision. Atlantis reports thickness readings, trends and flagged locations. Under API 510, 570 and 653 the owner's authorized inspector holds the responsibility for the program.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing accepted in place of radiography in Texas?
faq.a: It can be, when the governing code allows it and the owner, engineer and authorized inspector agree beforehand. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 contain their own provisions, so the contract decides.

faq.q: What affects the accuracy of a UT thickness reading?
faq.a: Surface roughness, scale, curvature, temperature, pitting, coating, calibration and the probe chosen all affect accuracy. Calibration on a step block of the same material and an A-scan check on doubtful readings reduce the risk of errors.

faq.q: Which ultrasonic code editions do you work to?
faq.a: We apply the edition named in your contract or procurement specification, whether that is ASME Section V, B31.3, Section VIII, API 1104 or AWS D1.1. If the contract is silent, we raise the question before work starts.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Dallas?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Dallas. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, so please tell us about site orientation, access equipment and permits when you request a quote.

faq.q: Can you examine welds on a construction site in Dallas?
faq.a: Yes. Weld examination is done where the steel is, provided the weld is accessible, the surface is cleaned and safe access is arranged. Please share the erection schedule so we can coordinate with the fabricator and the owner.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) & MPI | Dallas, TX
mt.description: Mag particle testing and magnetic particle inspection for Dallas, TX fabricators, rail, bridge and plant steel. Surface crack detection. Get an MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) in Dallas, Texas
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT offers magnetic particle testing in Dallas, Texas for fabricators, contractors, rail and utility owners and plant operators who need surface cracks found in carbon and low-alloy steel. This is the method for weld toes, fillet welds, lifting points, attachments and repair excavations. Technicians are mobilized to your shop, yard or site, use calibrated yokes and particles, and report each indication against the code you name. Request an MT quote for Dallas and we reply within one business day.

Dallas steel that gets examined by magnetic particle

Dallas is a metal-working metropolis. Fabrication shops cut and weld structural beams, columns, trusses, stairs and platforms for high-rise and warehouse construction across North Texas. Rail yards and car repair facilities handle couplers, bolsters, draft gear and welded car structures, where fatigue cracks start at surface stress concentrations. Overhead cranes in manufacturing plants and warehouses carry load every day through welded runway beams and hook blocks. Utility companies maintain transmission towers, substation steel and pole base connections.

All of these are made of ferromagnetic steel with welded attachments, and all can fail from a crack that began as a small surface discontinuity. Magnetic particle inspection is the quickest way to find those cracks on site without taking the part out of service or sending it to a laboratory.

The physics, and the materials it works on

A part is magnetized, and a discontinuity open to the surface or lying just beneath it distorts the field so some flux leaks into the air. Fine ferromagnetic particles dusted or sprayed on the surface collect at the leakage and outline the crack. The result is visible immediately and can be photographed.

That chain only works in ferromagnetic material. Carbon steel and most low-alloy steels respond well, while austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and brass do not, and for those parts liquid penetrant testing in Dallas is the right choice. The method is strongest at the surface and loses sensitivity rapidly with depth. A crack parallel to the field gives a weak or no signal, so a second examination is carried out with the field turned roughly ninety degrees. Coatings, scale and rust attenuate the result and are controlled by the procedure.

How the examination is carried out

Field work in Dallas relies mostly on portable electromagnetic yokes. ASME Section V Article 7 requires an AC yoke to show a lifting power of at least 10 pounds at the largest pole spacing used, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and these checks are made with a certified test weight. Prod methods push current through the part and can arc, which is prohibited on many pressure parts. Shop work on smaller components can use stationary equipment with coils or head-and-tail contact.

Particles can be dry powder, wet visible suspension or wet fluorescent suspension. Dry powder in a contrasting color is quick on outdoor structural welds. Fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light and a darkened enclosure, and they are used where fine cracks matter, such as crane components and critical lifting equipment. Demagnetization follows when a residual field would affect welding, machining or sensitive equipment. The technician records the technique, current or lift test, particle type and the area covered.

Codes that set acceptance in North Texas

Texas projects draw on a range of codes. AWS D1.1 includes magnetic particle acceptance rules for structural steel welds, AWS D1.5 covers bridges, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 sets methods and acceptance for pressure vessels. For process piping, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 and Table 341.3.2 apply. ASTM E709 and ASTM E1444 are the guide and practice often cited in specifications. Rail, crane and lifting gear programs may use owner standards or industry recommended practices.

For pressure equipment, the Texas Boiler Law is administered by the Department of Licensing and Regulation. Repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code with an authorized inspector. Under API 510, 570 and 653, the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record, and Atlantis reports indications without acting as that inspector. See the Texas inspection page, magnetic particle testing overview and the Article 7 explanation for more.

Who performs and reviews the work

Our MT technicians are qualified under the company written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II sets up and checks the equipment, performs the examination and interprets indications. An ASNT Level III approves the technique and reviews the report. Anoop Rayavarapu leads the Level III function; he holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Customers can have us follow their own written practice, or use written practice development if theirs needs updating. Related guidance is under Level III consulting.

The MT report

An MT report from Atlantis identifies the component and location, the procedure and revision, the equipment and its last lift or field check, the particle type and contrast method, the light levels and the technician and level. It lists each indication with position, length and orientation, with photographs or sketches, and states accept or reject against the named criteria. If demagnetization was needed, it records the residual field reading. If surfaces could not be examined because of access or coating, the report says what was left out.

Rail, crane and lifting-equipment programs

Many Dallas owners run periodic magnetic particle programs on equipment that carries load every day. A bridge crane in a manufacturing plant, for instance, may have its hook, trunnion and runway beam welds examined on a fixed schedule set by the owner's maintenance program or an industry standard, and a rail car shop may check couplers, bolsters and welded repairs when cars come in for service. These checks are valuable because fatigue cracks in such parts grow slowly at first and then quickly, and a periodic check catches them while the repair is still a grind-out and re-weld instead of a replacement.

To make the results comparable from one year to the next, the report identifies each location with a mark or a drawing reference, so the same weld can be examined again by the next technician. Where earlier reports exist, the technician reviews them before starting and notes any indication that has changed. If a crack is found, the report records its location and length, and the owner decides whether to grind it out, repair it or take the item out of service.

Weld repairs, grinding and re-examination

Magnetic particle inspection is a regular partner of weld repair. After a defect is ground out, the excavation is examined to confirm that the crack has been removed completely, and the examination is repeated after the repair weld is made and finished. This sequence matters because welding over a remaining crack tip simply buries the problem. The technician examines the full excavation and a margin around it, and records the result with a sketch of the area.

Where preheat or post-weld heat treatment applies, the timing of the examination follows the specification, since some steels develop delayed cracking and need a hold period before final inspection. Grinding marks and gouges can create their own false indications, so the technician smooths and cleans the area first. After the final examination, the part is demagnetized if the specification requires it, and all coatings that were removed are restored by the owner or the fabricator.

Common reasons MT results go wrong

Most poor magnetic particle results trace back to a short list of causes. A weak yoke, because the lift test was skipped or the poles are not seated flat, gives a field too faint to hold particles. Wrong field direction leaves a crack that lies along the field undetected. Over-application of particles buries a fine indication in powder, and too much contrast paint hides a crack from the field. Bad lighting, either dim white light or too much ambient light for fluorescent work, makes real indications hard to see. Dirty or oily surfaces keep particles from moving.

Each of these has a simple control: lift-test the yoke, examine in two directions, apply particles lightly, use a thin paint layer, measure the light and clean the surface. The technician uses a field indicator or pie gauge to check that the field is present, and records the checks. When a result is uncertain, the examination is repeated after cleaning instead of being reported as clear.

What to have ready before the technician arrives

A short checklist saves hours on site. Send the list of welds or components with drawing references, the code and edition that apply, and the acceptance criteria if they differ from the code. Say whether coatings must be removed and who will do it, whether scaffolding or lifts are needed, and what permits or safety training the site requires. If earlier inspection reports exist, include them so the technician can compare indications from one inspection to the next. Having power available matters for yokes with a mains supply, and so does a safe place to store particles, paint and cleaner.

Planning MT work in Dallas

Dallas weather is the planning variable. Summer heat makes steel too hot for some particle suspensions and contrast paints, and sunlight washes out UV-A indications, so work is moved to shaded areas or tented. Winter cold can slow wet particles and freeze suspensions, and ice storms can stop outdoor fabrication. Windy spring days blow dry powder away from the weld. The technician checks surface temperature and conditions before starting.

Site conditions matter as much. Construction sites ask for safety training and have changing access, fabrication yards have crane traffic, and rail properties have track safety rules that require escorts or flaggers. We mobilize technicians from outside the city and travel to your site, so please send gate and permit details with your request, along with the weld list and a drawing mark-up if you have one.

Choosing MT, UT or PT for your Dallas welds

For surface cracks in carbon steel welds, MT is typically the fastest field method. When you need to see whether a weld is sound all the way through or to measure remaining wall, add ultrasonic testing in Dallas. When the metal is stainless, use penetrant. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States; the radiographic testing page for Dallas explains the alternatives. The MT versus PT guide helps decide between the two surface methods.

Training your own MT technicians

Employers who want in-house capability can look at MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and magnetic particle testing training shows the content. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so these courses support your program. The Dallas training page gives delivery details, and the eligibility checker shows hours and vision requirements.

faq.q: Can MT inspect a weld that has been painted?
faq.a: Thin, tightly bonded paint is sometimes acceptable if the procedure has been shown to work through it. Thicker or flaking coatings are removed locally so the field reaches the steel and the particles can settle on a crack.

faq.q: Which Dallas components are checked by magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Typical items are structural weld toes and fillets, crane runway and hook structures, railcar welds, tower and substation steel, vessel attachments, weld repair excavations and any carbon steel part where surface cracking is the concern.

faq.q: Why does the yoke lifting power matter?
faq.a: It confirms the yoke produces a strong enough field. ASME Section V Article 7 requires 10 pounds for an AC yoke and 40 pounds for DC or permanent-magnet yokes at the maximum pole spacing, checked with a calibrated test weight.

faq.q: Is fluorescent magnetic particle inspection used in the field?
faq.a: Yes, when a darkened area can be created with covers or tents. UV-A light then reveals fine cracks. Outdoors in bright Dallas sunshine, dry visible powder with contrast paint is more common.

faq.q: What is demagnetization and when is it needed?
faq.a: Demagnetization removes the residual magnetic field left after inspection. It is needed when the field would disturb welding, machining, coating or nearby sensitive equipment, and the procedure or specification says when to do it.

faq.q: Can MT size a crack's depth?
faq.a: No. MT shows the length and location of surface indications but not depth. When depth matters for repair or fitness-for-service decisions, ultrasonic testing or controlled grinding with repeat checks is used.

faq.q: Will Atlantis sign off as the API 570 inspector?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record under API 570 and the other API codes. Atlantis performs the examination and reports the indications to the owner's inspector.

faq.q: Does Atlantis staff an office in Dallas?
faq.a: No. We have no Dallas office. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, so please include gate, safety orientation and permit details with your request.

faq.q: What do I need to supply for a Dallas MT job?
faq.a: Send the weld or component list, drawings or marked-up photographs, the governing code and edition, access arrangements and any site safety requirements. That is enough for us to scope the job and propose a procedure.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Dallas, TX | LPI
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for Dallas, TX stainless, aluminum and steel parts, welds and repairs. Request a PT quote now.
pt.h1: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Dallas, Texas
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out dye penetrant inspection, formally liquid penetrant testing or PT, in Dallas, Texas. Use it on welds, castings, machined parts and repairs in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel when you need surface-breaking cracks found without a magnet. Technicians are mobilized to your shop, plant or site and work to your procedure or one written to the governing code. Request a PT quote for Dallas and we reply within one business day.

What gets penetrant-tested in the Dallas area

The Dallas economy produces a wide mix of materials that magnets cannot test. Food, beverage, pharmaceutical and chemical plants use stainless steel piping, tanks and heat exchangers with sanitary and corrosion-resistant welds. Aerospace and defense suppliers in the Metroplex machine and weld aluminum, titanium and nickel alloys. Commercial buildings and hospitals have stainless and copper piping and stainless boiler and chiller components. Fabricators weld aluminum structures and stainless platforms, and machine shops produce castings and forgings that need a surface check before delivery.

For all of these, penetrant testing is the practical surface method. It is also used on carbon steel when a yoke will not fit, on non-magnetic overlay, and as the final check after grinding out a crack to confirm the excavation is clean.

How penetrant testing detects flaws

A low-viscosity liquid is applied to a clean, dry surface and given time to be drawn into any opening by capillary action. The excess is removed, and a thin layer of developer pulls the trapped liquid back to the surface, where it spreads into a visible indication. Visible penetrant shows as red against a white developer background; fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light and gives a higher sensitivity for fine cracks.

The same principle defines the limits. Only discontinuities that are open to the surface can be found, so subsurface flaws need ultrasonic testing. Surfaces smeared by grinding, peening, blasting or machining can close a crack and hide it, and porous or very rough surfaces hold liquid and make indications hard to read. Cleanliness is the largest source of error, because oil, paint, scale or residual cleaning solvent blocks the opening. Our ultrasonic testing page for Dallas covers the volumetric option, and magnetic particle inspection in Dallas covers carbon steel surface cracks.

Penetrant systems and technique

Penetrants are classified by color (visible or fluorescent) and by removal method: water washable, post-emulsifiable or solvent removable. Dallas field work mostly uses solvent-removable visible systems because they are portable and need no darkened space. Shop work on critical parts may use fluorescent water-washable or post-emulsified systems for higher sensitivity. For stainless steel and nickel alloys, materials with controlled chlorine and sulfur content are specified, and the lot numbers are recorded.

The steps are precise: pre-clean and dry, apply penetrant, dwell for the time given in the procedure, remove the excess without washing out the cracks, apply developer in a thin even layer, wait the development time and examine under adequate light. The technician watches the indications as they develop, because they change with time. Afterward, residual materials are removed when the procedure requires post-cleaning, which matters for parts going into food, medical or oxygen service.

Temperature in a city of extremes

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the standard temperature range for the part and materials at 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside it, the procedure must be qualified at the actual temperature. Dallas gives both problems. In summer, steel in sunlight can exceed 125 degrees by a wide margin, which dries penetrant and bakes developer before they work, and the part must be shaded and allowed to cool or a qualified high-temperature procedure used. In winter, a hard freeze can bring surface temperature below 40 degrees, slowing penetrant and forming condensation or frost, so enclosures, heaters or a cold-qualified procedure are needed.

The technician measures surface temperature with a contact or non-contact thermometer before starting and records it in the report. If conditions are outside the range, the work waits or the procedure changes. A quick test on a known-flaw comparator block can verify performance at borderline temperatures.

Codes and acceptance for Texas work

The method is defined in ASME Section V Article 6, and ASTM E165 and ASTM E1417 are common references in specifications. Acceptance comes from the governing code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 covers penetrant methods and acceptance for pressure vessels, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 with Table 341.3.2 for process piping. For structural and bridge welding, AWS D1.1 and D1.5 set their own surface requirements, and AWS D1.6 covers stainless structural welds. Rounded and linear indications are evaluated separately by size and spacing.

In Texas, boiler and pressure vessel repairs follow the National Board Inspection Code, and the Department of Licensing and Regulation administers the Texas Boiler Law. Under API 510 and 570, the owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record, and Atlantis provides the examination results. The Texas inspection page covers the process, with background in penetrant testing and the Article 6 explainer.

Qualified technicians and procedures

PT technicians work under the company written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II applies the process and interprets, while an ASNT Level III writes or approves the procedure and reviews the report. Anoop Rayavarapu runs the Level III side and holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. If your company has its own written practice or customer procedure, we follow it. For help drafting one, see written practice development and Level III consulting.

What the penetrant report contains

The report records the component and location, the procedure and revision, the penetrant, remover and developer by product and batch, the surface temperature, dwell and development times, the lighting, the technician and level, and each indication with position, size and a photograph. The report closes with an accept or reject decision against the criteria you named. Where a surface could not be examined or was in doubtful condition, the report says so rather than presenting a clean result.

Checking the process before and during the job

A penetrant examination is only as reliable as the process behind it, so the technician checks it before trusting results. A comparator block with known cracks, or a similar reference, can be used to confirm that the penetrant and developer in use are working at the surface temperature on the day. If the known cracks do not show, the materials, the technique or the conditions are corrected before the part is examined. Materials are checked for expiry and contamination, and aerosol cans are discarded if they have been left in the sun or frozen.

During the job, the technician keeps to the dwell and development times in the procedure and does not hurry them. Adequate lighting is checked with a meter: visible indications need white light at the level the procedure requires, and fluorescent indications need UV-A light and low ambient white light. If a part is large, the area is examined in sections so that no part dries out before it has been read.

Common penetrant problems and how they are handled

A few problems show up repeatedly. Over-removal, where excess penetrant is wiped with too much solvent, can pull liquid out of a real crack, so the technician wipes with a lightly dampened cloth. Under-removal leaves a pink background that hides indications. A thick or uneven developer coat can mask fine cracks or run into a blur. Rough weld caps and porous castings hold penetrant and give a broad background, in which case the surface is dressed or another method is chosen. Contaminated surfaces keep penetrant from entering at all.

Each problem is handled in the procedure and in practice: clean thoroughly, dwell for the right time, remove carefully, apply developer thinly, and re-test an area if the first result is doubtful. When the surface prevents a trustworthy examination, the report says so and suggests dressing the surface or using another technique, instead of passing the part on a poor test.

Parts and welds in Dallas supply chains

Machine shops and fabricators around Dallas often need penetrant results as part of a deliverable to a customer, and the report becomes a quality record. Typical cases include weld joints on stainless piping, machined housings and flanges, aluminum structural welds, repaired castings and the final surface of overlay or cladding. The technician matches the penetrant system to the job, whether that is a portable solvent-removable kit for a field weld or a fluorescent system on a bench for small parts, and writes the report so the customer can attach it to the quality file without rework.

Where a customer's purchase order names a specification, the report cites the clauses, the method and the acceptance criteria used, so the record is traceable. If the order is silent, we ask which code or customer standard applies before starting, because acceptance criteria for a machined part and for a structural weld are not the same.

Planning a PT job in Dallas

The main planning item is surface preparation. Machined parts need to be free of cutting fluid, and welded areas need spatter and slag removed. If grinding or blasting has been done, an etch may be needed to open smeared metal. For stainless steel, avoid carbon steel brushes and chloride-bearing cleaners, because contamination causes later corrosion. Allow time for solvent to evaporate before applying penetrant.

On site, ask for shade in summer and wind protection in spring, and for a heated enclosure when it freezes. Many Dallas facilities require safety orientation and badges, and some, such as food or pharmaceutical plants, restrict chemicals. We mobilize technicians from outside the city and travel to your site, so tell us early about chemical approvals, clean-room rules or outage dates.

PT, MT or UT for your Dallas parts

Choose penetrant for non-magnetic material or when a magnet is not practical, magnetic particle for quick, sensitive surface checks on carbon steel, and ultrasonic testing when depth or volume matters. Stainless welds are often checked with penetrant on the surface and ultrasonic testing for the body. Radiography is not something Atlantis performs in the United States; see the radiographic testing page for Dallas for alternatives. For a side-by-side view of surface methods, read MT versus PT.

Training penetrant technicians

For in-house capability, PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training cover the skills, penetrant testing training describes the outline, and the penetrant testing simulator gives practice. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. See the Dallas training page for delivery.

faq.q: Is dye penetrant inspection the same as liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. Dye penetrant describes the visible-dye version of liquid penetrant testing. Fluorescent penetrant is the other main type, and both follow the same steps of cleaning, applying, removing excess and developing.

faq.q: Which metals can be tested with penetrant in Dallas?
faq.a: Penetrant works on stainless steel, aluminum, titanium, nickel alloys, copper alloys and carbon steel, provided the surface is non-porous and clean. It is the standard surface method for non-magnetic material.

faq.q: What temperature range is allowed for PT?
faq.a: The standard range under ASME Section V Article 6 is 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for part and materials. Outside it the procedure must be qualified, which matters on sun-heated steel and in winter freezes.

faq.q: Why can grinding or blasting hide a crack from penetrant?
faq.a: Grinding, peening or blasting can smear metal across the opening of a crack, closing it. A light etch or controlled cleaning restores the opening before penetrant is applied.

faq.q: Can penetrant be used on parts for food or oxygen service?
faq.a: Yes, with care. Materials are selected for compatibility and residues are removed afterward under a post-clean step. Tell us about service requirements so the procedure and cleaning match them.

faq.q: What causes a false or masked indication?
faq.a: Residual oil, paint, cleaner or penetrant bleed-out from rough surfaces can create false patterns, and dried penetrant or heavy developer can mask a real one. Cleaning, timing and thin developer coats prevent most errors.

faq.q: Can Atlantis serve as the API 570 inspector for PT work?
faq.a: No. The owner's authorized inspector is the inspector of record under API 570. Atlantis does the penetrant examination and gives the results to that inspector.

faq.q: Does Atlantis maintain an office in Dallas?
faq.a: No. We have no Dallas office. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, so please tell us about badging, chemical restrictions and access when you ask for a quote.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Dallas, TX | RT Alternatives
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. See ultrasonic testing alternatives and Level III radiograph review for Dallas, TX projects.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) in Dallas, Texas: What Atlantis Offers
rt.html:
Radiographic work in Dallas is outside what Atlantis does: the company does not perform radiography anywhere in the United States. Industrial radiography is licensed work under the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and Texas is an Agreement State with its own licensing. It is not a service we offer in Dallas. If your specification requires radiography on structural, piping or pressure equipment welds, you will need a licensed radiography contractor, and we do not recommend any. We can help with ultrasonic examination where the code permits it, with independent review of images, and with training theory.

Ultrasonic testing where the code allows it

Many Dallas projects name radiography by habit, not necessity. ASME B31.3 contains provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds in process piping, API 1104 provides for it on pipeline girth welds, and AWS D1.1 gives ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds in structural steel, which covers a large share of Metroplex construction. ASME Section VIII permits ultrasonic testing in place of radiography only under specific conditions. In every case the change is agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before work starts, and it is written into the procedure.

Where it is accepted, shear-wave ultrasonic examination sees lack of fusion and cracks well and requires no radiation exclusion area, so adjacent trades can keep working on a busy construction site. See ultrasonic testing in Dallas for how the work is carried out.

Level III review of radiographs and procedures

Looking at an image does not require a radiation licence. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital radiographs and the technique sheets that go with them against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, give a second read when a fabricator and an owner disagree about an indication, and check a radiography contractor's procedure or written practice for gaps. Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, would carry out that review.

This is a paper-and-image service. Nothing is exposed by us, and we do not countersign a contractor's work. It suits owners who want an independent opinion before accepting a package, and fabricators who want a second look at a rejected weld. For related support see Level III consulting and written practice development.

Surface methods we perform in Dallas

Some welds only need a surface check, and two methods cover that. Magnetic particle inspection in Dallas finds surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, and liquid penetrant testing in Dallas does the same for stainless steel, aluminum and non-magnetic alloys. They do not replace a volumetric requirement in the code, but they remove surface defects before a licensed contractor shoots the weld.

Radiography theory and training

The RT Level 2 course covers theory and film interpretation for employers who qualify their own staff under SNT-TC-1A. The employer certifies the technician, and handling sources or x-ray equipment still needs the licences and radiation safety training required by the state. See the Dallas training page for how sessions run.

Sending us your Dallas request

Tell us the code and edition, weld type, thickness range and the exact wording in your specification. If it requires radiography with no alternative, you will need a licensed contractor, and we can still review the output. If ultrasonic examination is allowed, we can propose a procedure for your owner's approval. Ask about RT alternatives for Dallas and we reply within one business day. Ultrasonic technicians are mobilized to your site, and the Texas inspection page adds context.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing available from Atlantis in Dallas?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because it is a licensed activity under NRC rules or Agreement State rules. We offer ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant testing, plus Level III image review.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a Dallas structural weld?
faq.a: It can where the governing code and the owner allow it. AWS D1.1 has ultrasonic criteria for groove welds, and ASME B31.3 and API 1104 have their own provisions. Agree the substitution with the owner and engineer first.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs taken by another company?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the code, and can give a second opinion on disputed indications. We do not take new exposures.

faq.q: Do you recommend radiography contractors in the Dallas area?
faq.a: No. We do not name or recommend radiography contractors. The Texas regulator can confirm whether a company is licensed, and we can review the contractor's procedure and written practice on request.

faq.q: Does Atlantis teach radiography?
faq.a: Our RT Level 2 course covers theory for employers who certify their own staff under SNT-TC-1A. Working with sources or x-ray equipment still requires state licences and radiation safety training.
